newsitem.title: INDIA: India mulling plans to mark 50 years of freedom.
newsitem.headline: India mulling plans to mark 50 years of freedom.

text.p: India said on Monday it was considering a vast array of proposals to commemorate 50 years of freedom from colonial rule, including a plan to erect a statue of Mahatma Gandhi -- in Antarctica.
"There is one such proposal that the government is considering," Human Resource Development Minister S.R. Bommai told a news conference.
He was responding to a questioner asking why the government had chosen Antarctica when there was not a single prominent statue of the spiritual father of independent India in New Delhi.
"We have not taken any decision on it," Bommai added hastily.

India attained freedom from British colonial rule on August 15, 1947. Celebrations to mark the anniversary will include enactments of historical events, including a special session of parliament at midnight on August 14 to simulate independent India's first parliamentary session, Bommai said.

For two days, the government will waive a law banning ordinary citizens from flying the national flag and encourage people to hoist the saffron, white and green flag on their homes and cars on August 14 and 15, Bommai said.

"The central idea is that every citizen should remember we are celebrating the 50th anniversary of independence throughout the year, and it should rekindle the spirit and values of the freedom struggle," the minister said.

While many countries had already started marking India's 50th year of independence through cultural exchange programmes, New Delhi planned to commemorate the occasion in the year starting August 15, 1997, he said.

The celebrations will cost the government some 510 million rupees ($14.25 million). In addition to three committees and 10 advisory groups, the federal government has set up an 88-member Secretariat for the Commemoration of the 50th Anniversary of Indian Independence.
Bommai said the government had received more than 2,000 suggestions from the public on how to celebrate the anniversary.

These included parades, starting a site on the Internet, releasing an audio tape of speeches by prominent Indian leaders, broadcasting Mahatma Gandhi's favourite hymns on state-run media and requesting every family in the 930 million-strong nation to light a candle at a specified time on August 15.
